note: Methodology as data (Analysis Layer 3, Phase 7). One entry per canonical metric of docs/analysis-layer-2/02-metric-registry.md plus the composites and Layer 3 engines. Read by the Node tests, the console and, copied as an asset, the Android app. kind: raw | derived | modeled | inferred | composite. A modeled/inferred entry needs a reference or productDefined=true; a composite is always productDefined. Citations are primary sources only.

metrics.methodology: Per-sample heart rate as reported by the watch. For Zepp workouts the per-second series is stored with the workout (zepp_workout_detail.decoded) and drawn on the session's chart, colour-coded by zone; the workout's seconds per bpm are also kept as a small histogram for the weekly intensity split. Other sessions keep only session-level and daily aggregates; Health Connect series are read on demand.
limitations: Optical heart-rate sensors lose accuracy during high-intensity, irregular-motion and cold-weather activity.
Sessions without a Zepp record have no stored per-sample series.

metrics.methodology: Mean heart rate over a recorded exercise session, as reported by Health Connect or the Zepp extract. Never recomputed.
limitations: Depends on the watch's sensor and sampling interval.
Averages hide interval structure; compare like with like sessions.

metrics.methodology: Highest heart rate in a recorded session, as reported by the source. Never recomputed.
limitations: A single optical spike or cadence-lock artefact can set the maximum.
Often missing for manually entered sessions.

metrics.methodology: Daily heart-rate variability as reported by the device. Evaluated elsewhere as ln(HRV): the 7-day rolling mean against your own 60-day baseline, with a band of half the baseline standard deviation (the smallest worthwhile change) and a 7-day coefficient of variation as an instability signal.
limitations: Whether the vendor value is rMSSD or SDNN is not confirmed for every source.
Vendor algorithms, firmware and sleep-stage classification change over time; a change of device or source can shift the series without any physiological change (see series breaks).
Single nights are noisy; only the 7-day trend is judged.

references.citation: Plews DJ, Laursen PB, Stanley J, Kilding AE, Buchheit M. Training adaptation and heart rate variability in elite endurance athletes: opening the door to effective monitoring. Sports Med 2013;43(9):773-781.
Shaffer F, Ginsberg JP. An overview of heart rate variability metrics and norms. Front Public Health 2017;5:258.

metrics.methodology: Daily resting heart rate as reported by the device. Evaluated with the same band structure as HRV but without the log transform: 7-day mean against your 60-day baseline, band of half the baseline standard deviation.
limitations: Vendors define 'resting' differently (lowest sleeping value, lowest rolling average, quiet-wake value).
Illness, alcohol, late meals and heat raise it for reasons unrelated to training.

references.citation: Hopkins WG, Marshall SW, Batterham AM, Hanin J. Progressive statistics for studies in sports medicine and exercise science. Med Sci Sports Exerc 2009;41(1):3-13.

metrics.methodology: Vendor-estimated maximal oxygen uptake, reported intermittently after qualifying outdoor efforts. Shown as received; the app does not estimate it itself.
limitations: A watch estimate, not a laboratory test; typical error is several ml/kg/min.
Updates only after suitable efforts, so it lags real changes.

metrics.methodology: Duration of a recorded or manually logged session in minutes, as stored.
limitations: Auto-paused time may or may not be included depending on the source.

metrics.methodology: Distance of a session in kilometres, as reported by the source (GPS) or typed in.
limitations: GPS distance is under- or over-estimated in tunnels, dense cover and on tracks with tight turns.

metrics.methodology: Minutes per kilometre = duration / distance, computed when the source gives no average speed.
limitations: Inherits any error in distance and duration.
An average hides pacing and stops.

metrics.methodology: Average speed in km/h as reported by Health Connect, or distance divided by duration for manual entries.
limitations: Same GPS limits as distance.

metrics.methodology: Average power in watts from a power meter or the watch's running-power estimate, as reported.
limitations: Vendor running-power models are not comparable across brands.
Rarely populated in this account's data.

metrics.methodology: Steps or revolutions per minute. Not stored by the app today.
limitations: No ingestion path exists yet.

metrics.methodology: Total ascent in metres for a session as reported by the source.
limitations: Barometric and GPS altitude differ; GPS-only ascent is usually overstated.

metrics.methodology: Your own rating of perceived exertion for a session on a 0 to 10 scale, entered after the session.
limitations: Subjective and scale-anchoring varies between people and over time.
Missing for most sessions that were not logged by hand.

references.citation: Foster C, Florhaug JA, Franklin J, et al. A new approach to monitoring exercise training. J Strength Cond Res 2001;15(1):109-115.

metrics.methodology: Reps in reserve per set. Not stored today.
limitations: No column exists yet.

metrics.methodology: Sets, repetitions and load in kilograms per exercise as typed into a strength session.
limitations: Entered by hand; edit-only after the fact.
Load does not capture tempo, range of motion or rest.

metrics.methodology: Hours of the main sleep period as reported by the source. Evaluated with the same band structure as HRV: 7-day mean against your own 60-day baseline, band of half the baseline standard deviation. Main sleeps under 2 hours are treated as a recording fault, not a night.
limitations: Wrist-worn sleep detection mistakes quiet wakefulness for sleep and may split a night.
Source changes can alter duration without any change in your sleep.

references.citation: Hirshkowitz M, Whiton K, Albert SM, et al. National Sleep Foundation's sleep time duration recommendations: methodology and results summary. Sleep Health 2015;1(1):40-43.

metrics.methodology: Minutes in deep, REM and light sleep as classified by the device. Each stage is evaluated against your own 60-day baseline exactly like sleep duration.
limitations: Wrist devices infer stages from movement and pulse, not brain activity; agreement with polysomnography is moderate and varies by stage.
A firmware or algorithm update can shift stage minutes abruptly (see series breaks).

metrics.methodology: Breaths per minute during sleep as reported by the device. An anomaly flag compares recent nights with your own baseline.
limitations: Estimated from heart-rate and motion signals, not measured at the airway.
Sparse in this account's data.

metrics.methodology: Probability, rescaled to -100..100, that you are in the same state (asleep or awake) at any clock minute as 24 hours earlier. Computed on 5-minute bins over at least 14 nights; more than 2 missing nights in a row returns 'building' instead of a number.
limitations: Needs consecutive nights; gaps degrade it.
Treats naps and split sleep as ordinary sleep time.

references.citation: Phillips AJK, Clerx WM, O'Brien CS, et al. Irregular sleep/wake patterns are associated with poorer academic performance and delayed circadian and sleep/wake timing. Sci Rep 2017;7:3216.

metrics.methodology: Body mass in kilograms as weighed or imported.
limitations: Day-to-day change is dominated by water, food and bowel contents.

metrics.methodology: Exponentially weighted moving average of body weight, time-aware so a skipped day does not distort the trend. The smoothing constant is chosen from how often you weigh in over the last 30 days. A 'stable' call needs at least 10 measurements over 14 days and a slope under 0.15 kg per week.
limitations: Lags a real change by the smoothing time.
Sparse weigh-ins make the trend unreliable.

metrics.methodology: Body fat percentage from a bioelectrical-impedance reading. Two readings are compared only when at least 30 days apart and the difference exceeds a least significant change.
limitations: Impedance readings vary with hydration, food and time of day; noise can exceed the real change over weeks.
Not interchangeable with DEXA.

references.citation: Hopkins WG. Measures of reliability in sports medicine and science. Sports Med 2000;30(1):1-15.

metrics.methodology: Lean mass in kilograms from the same impedance reading, as reported.
limitations: Same hydration sensitivity as body fat %; sparse in this account's data.

metrics.methodology: Nutrient amounts per meal. Amounts for logged foods come from a food database through a deterministic resolver; a model never supplies nutrient values.
limitations: Database entries are averages for a food, not your portion or brand.
Portion size is the largest source of error.

metrics.methodology: Daily fluid volume in millilitres. Each non-water drink also carries an effective-hydration estimate from a fixed per-beverage retention factor (model v1).
limitations: Counts what you log, not what you drink.
Retention factors are population values from one study, not personal.

references.citation: Maughan RJ, Watson P, Cordery PAA, et al. A randomized trial to assess the potential of different beverages to affect hydration status: development of a beverage hydration index. Am J Clin Nutr 2016;103(3):717-723.

metrics.methodology: Grams of pure ethanol = volume in ml x strength (ABV %) / 100 x 0.789 g/ml, rounded to 0.1 g. The strength must be stated; a drink without one is not recorded. Never derived from calories.
limitations: Labelled strength can differ from the actual pour.
Home pours and mixed drinks are estimates.

references.citation: National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism. What is a standard drink? (14 g of pure alcohol in the United States).

metrics.methodology: Your own 0 to 10 ratings of energy, mood, stress and soreness for a day. Scores are treated as ordered categories, not interval measurements.
limitations: Subjective; the same number can mean different things on different days.
Only days you logged exist; missing days are not zero.

references.citation: Saw AE, Main LC, Gastin PB. Monitoring the athlete training response: subjective self-reported measures trump commonly used objective measures: a systematic review. Br J Sports Med 2016;50(5):281-291.

metrics.methodology: Session load = minutes x RPE when an RPE was logged, otherwise Banister's TRIMP from average heart rate against the person's maximum and resting heart rate as of the session's date (see TRIMP); a session with neither contributes nothing, nothing is imputed. Loads are summed per day. Fitness (CTL) and fatigue (ATL) are exponentially weighted averages with spans of 42 and 7 days (alpha = 2 / (span + 1)), and form (TSB) is yesterday's CTL minus ATL. Since October 2026 the spans can be your own: every night a pair is fitted to forecast tomorrow morning's ln HRV (from today's ln HRV, the weekday, fitness and fatigue) and tested on weeks the fit never saw (rolling origin, log score); it replaces 42 and 7, in the app and the console alike, only when it forecasts better (the 95% Newey-West interval of the daily score difference above zero, the PREDICTIVE rung). CTL needs 42 days of history.
limitations: The spans are population conventions unless your own pair beat them on held-out weeks, and a personal pair is fitted to HRV, not to performance.
Sessions with neither an RPE nor heart rate understate load.
The web dashboard still computes a different ratio (ACWR) from the same sessions.

references.citation: Banister EW, Calvert TW, Savage MV, Bach TM. A systems model of training for athletic performance. Aust J Sports Med 1975;7:57-61.
Foster C, Florhaug JA, Franklin J, et al. A new approach to monitoring exercise training. J Strength Cond Res 2001;15(1):109-115.
Gneiting T, Raftery AE. Strictly proper scoring rules, prediction, and estimation. J Am Stat Assoc 2007;102(477):359-378.
Tashman LJ. Out-of-sample tests of forecasting accuracy: an analysis and review. Int J Forecast 2000;16(4):437-450.

metrics.methodology: Banister's training impulse: minutes x heart-rate-reserve fraction x 0.64 x e^(1.92 x fraction), with the fraction (average - resting) / (maximum - resting) capped at 1. The maximum and resting heart rate are the person's as of the session's date: the second-highest session maximum of the 24 months up to it (so one optical spike cannot set it) and the 30-day median resting heart rate. It is the load of every session without an RPE. Until October 2026 the fraction divided by the session's own maximum, which made easy sessions score about twice what they should.
limitations: Average heart rate hides how the session was spread: an interval session and a steady one with the same average score alike.
Male coefficients (0.64, 1.92) are used for everyone; the female pair (0.86, 1.67) is not applied yet.
The maximum is the highest values the watch saw, not a tested maximum, and drifts with what the sessions reached.

references.citation: Banister EW, Calvert TW. Planning for future performance: implications for long term training. Can J Appl Sport Sci 1980;5(3):170-176.

Banister EW. Modeling elite athletic performance. In: MacDougall JD, Wenger HA, Green HJ, eds. Physiological Testing of the High-Performance Athlete. 2nd ed. Champaign, IL: Human Kinetics; 1991:403-424.

metrics.methodology: Session intensity as a percentage of a personal threshold. Not implemented: no threshold profile exists.
limitations: Requires a measured threshold heart rate, pace or power.

metrics.methodology: RPE x session minutes.
limitations: Inherits the subjectivity of RPE.
Does not distinguish a hard short session from an easy long one with the same product.

references.citation: Foster C, Florhaug JA, Franklin J, et al. A new approach to monitoring exercise training. J Strength Cond Res 2001;15(1):109-115.

metrics.methodology: A blood or urine result with its unit and the laboratory's reference range. A change between two draws is judged against the marker's reference change value, which combines analytical and within-person biological variation.
limitations: Roughly one draw a year gives two-point comparisons, never a trend.
Reference ranges are population ranges, not optimal ranges.

references.citation: Fraser CG, Harris EK. Generation and application of data on biological variation in clinical chemistry. Crit Rev Clin Lab Sci 1989;27(5):409-437.

metrics.methodology: Your own 0 to 10 severity rating for a logged injury or illness. Weekly health-problem screening uses the OSTRC questionnaire.
limitations: Self-rated; not a diagnosis.

references.citation: Clarsen B, Ronsen O, Myklebust G, Florenes TW, Bahr R. The Oslo Sports Trauma Research Center questionnaire on health problems: a new approach to prospective monitoring of illness and injury in elite athletes. Br J Sports Med 2014;48(9):754-760.

metrics.methodology: A 0 to 100 index that aggregates the existing sleep evaluations (duration, regularity, respiratory anomaly, stages) with named fixed weights. It shows how close your recent week is to your own norm, never a universal target: duration and stages count against their own 60-day means, capped at 100. At least two components are required. One set of cut-offs, shared with Today's recovery: AS EXPECTED from 75, BELOW EXPECTED under 75, UNUSUALLY LOW under 55; it has no ABOVE EXPECTED, since a week cannot score better than its own norm. Since October 2026 it carries a scorecard worked out on your own history: every past morning it is recomputed as it would have read then and turned into a forecast of the day's energy and that morning's HRV against its recent level by a straight line fitted only on the days before (the last 120 with an outcome); the forecast is scored once the outcome is known (log score of a Gaussian forecast), and each of its single inputs is scored the same way on the same days. It EARNS ITS PLACE when it beats its best single input (the 95% Newey-West interval of the daily score difference above zero), is NO BETTER when it cannot be more than negligibly better, and then is shown as its inputs, without its own word (INPUTS ONLY); otherwise UNCLEAR, or NOT YET SCORED before 60 scored days. It is demoted only when it is no better on both outcomes; its main rival is last night's duration alone.
limitations: Product-defined: weights are documented opinions, not fitted or clinically validated.
Not comparable between people.
The 75 and 55 cut-offs are product-defined.

references.citation: Gneiting T, Raftery AE. Strictly proper scoring rules, prediction, and estimation. J Am Stat Assoc 2007;102(477):359-378.
Diebold FX, Mariano RS. Comparing predictive accuracy. J Bus Econ Stat 1995;13(3):253-263.
Tashman LJ. Out-of-sample tests of forecasting accuracy: an analysis and review. Int J Forecast 2000;16(4):437-450.

metrics.methodology: A recovery state built from separate contributors (the Sleep Index, HRV and resting heart rate as 7-day against 60-day baselines, training load, energy, stress and soreness, optionally Zepp stress). Each keeps its own direction and confidence; they are listed, not blended into one score. At least two contributors are required for a state: ABOVE EXPECTED when every contributor with a direction points up, BELOW EXPECTED when every one points down, MIXED SIGNALS when they disagree, AS EXPECTED otherwise. The Sleep Index counts with its own cut-offs: as expected (75 or more) it is neutral, below that it holds recovery back. Since October 2026 it carries a scorecard worked out on your own history: every past morning it is recomputed as it would have read then and turned into a forecast of tomorrow morning's HRV against its recent level by a straight line fitted only on the days before (the last 120 with an outcome); the forecast is scored once the outcome is known (log score of a Gaussian forecast), and each of its single inputs is scored the same way on the same days. It EARNS ITS PLACE when it beats its best single input (the 95% Newey-West interval of the daily score difference above zero), is NO BETTER when it cannot be more than negligibly better, and then is shown as its inputs, without its own word (INPUTS ONLY); otherwise UNCLEAR, or NOT YET SCORED before 60 scored days.
limitations: Product-defined, not clinically validated.
Direction mapping (for example lower resting heart rate is better) is a convention.
The scorecard's history leaves out the Zepp stress contributor, which exists only for the last few days.
READY FOR is the same state matched to the demand of a kind of session; its own scorecard asks whether planned sessions were done (Brier score), and needs 40 planned days.

references.citation: Gneiting T, Raftery AE. Strictly proper scoring rules, prediction, and estimation. J Am Stat Assoc 2007;102(477):359-378.
Diebold FX, Mariano RS. Comparing predictive accuracy. J Bus Econ Stat 1995;13(3):253-263.
Tashman LJ. Out-of-sample tests of forecasting accuracy: an analysis and review. Int J Forecast 2000;16(4):437-450.

metrics.methodology: A binary-segmentation scan for a lasting change in the level or the spread of a daily series, with an allowance for day-to-day autocorrelation. A detected break is only a candidate: a baseline restarts when the data source changed within 3 days of it or you confirm that the device or source changed.
limitations: Real physiological changes look the same as source changes; that is why confirmation is required.
Location is only as precise as the data density.
A critical value of 6 gave a 0.7 % false-alarm rate in simulation; real data may differ.

metrics.methodology: A fixed catalogue of questions (for example alcohol and next-morning HRV), each tested once with one regression: the outcome on day t against the exposure on day t minus the lag, adjusted for weekday, a slow trend (a linear spline with a knot every 60 days), the outcome measured before the exposure and the exposure behind that earlier outcome. Standard errors are Newey-West in calendar days with small-sample corrections, so neighbouring days are not counted as independent. The verdict compares the 95% interval with the question's no-effect zone, fixed before any data (HRV 2%, resting heart rate 1 bpm, sleep 10 minutes, energy half a point): CLEAR when the interval lies entirely outside the zone, NEGLIGIBLE when it lies entirely inside, UNCLEAR when it crosses an edge, NOT YET when there are too few days. Each answer carries the smallest effect the data could detect, an E-value and a negative-control lag (the same model on the outcome before the exposure). On simulated data with no effect, under 1% of questions read clear; planted effects are covered by the 95% interval 93-96% of the time. Because every question is re-checked every night, the verdict uses a repeated confidence interval with an O'Brien-Fleming-type boundary (2.24 divided by the square root of the information so far against a full year), so with no effect a question reads clear at some point in about 1% of simulated histories instead of 10%. Every verdict is kept in an append-only ledger. Questions about the same exposure are also pooled (normal-normal model, DerSimonian-Laird spread) and the pooled estimate is shown next to the verdict.
limitations: Observational: a clear answer is an association on the evidence ladder's second rung, not proof of cause; only a randomised self-experiment reaches 'tested'.

Days without a record are left out, except where a question states that absence counts as none (an answered evening check-in, days with a watch record for training, days after the first logged recovery session).

If the exposure follows your state (you drink on good days), adjusting for the morning before helps but cannot remove all of it; the negative-control lag warns when the outcome already differed before the exposure.
Product-defined catalogue and no-effect zones: the questions and zones were chosen in advance, not discovered from your data.

references.citation: Newey WK, West KD. A simple, positive semi-definite, heteroskedasticity and autocorrelation consistent covariance matrix. Econometrica 1987;55(3):703-708.
Lakens D, Scheel AM, Isager PM. Equivalence testing for psychological research: a tutorial. Adv Methods Pract Psychol Sci 2018;1(2):259-269.
VanderWeele TJ, Ding P. Sensitivity analysis in observational research: introducing the E-value. Ann Intern Med 2017;167(4):268-274.
Lipsitch M, Tchetgen Tchetgen E, Cohen T. Negative controls: a tool for detecting confounding and bias in observational studies. Epidemiology 2010;21(3):383-388.
Lan KKG, DeMets DL. Discrete sequential boundaries for clinical trials. Biometrika 1983;70(3):659-663.
DerSimonian R, Laird N. Meta-analysis in clinical trials. Control Clin Trials 1986;7(3):177-188.

metrics.methodology: Compares today with your own recent typical days across five signals together: ln HRV, resting heart rate, sleep hours, deep + REM minutes and steps. The baseline is up to 120 past days that ends before the 14 days being judged, leaves out logged illness days and starts at the last confirmed series break. Each signal is standardised with a robust centre and spread (median, MAD); the joint pattern is described by a mean and a Ledoit-Wolf shrunk covariance, so correlated signals are judged together. A day's distance is the Mahalanobis distance over the signals it has (at least three) divided by their number, and 'elevated' and 'unusual' mean further out than 90% and 97.5% of your own typical days (leave-one-out). Two such days in a row with resting heart rate up suggest logging an illness. Today's steps are ignored because the day is not over, and a device-sensitive signal (deep + REM) is left out while a detected series break lies inside the window. Since October 2026 its strain flag is scored against logged illness: the engine is replayed two weeks at a time on your history, each block against the baseline before it, and each strain day outside an illness is checked against illnesses logged in the three days after. Precision (strain days followed by an illness) is set against the base rate (the share of all days that fall in the three days before one): EARNS ITS PLACE when the precision's 95% Wilson interval lies above the base rate, NO BETTER THAN CHANCE when it lies under one and a half times it, UNCLEAR otherwise, NOT YET SCORED before 5 logged illnesses and 10 strain days.
limitations: Experimental: on a real 9-month history, replayed one day at a time, it flagged clearly more ordinary days than its nominal 10% (elevated) and 2.5% (unusual), because real signals drift and change regime; on synthetic stationary data it stays near nominal. It is therefore shown as a drill-down and does not feed Today's Recovery.
A day being atypical is not a problem in itself (an unusually long sleep or a big hike day are atypical too); only the strain flag requires resting heart rate to be up.
Needs 45 complete days (all five signals) before it says anything.
Observational and personal: it says nothing about other people or about causes.
The scorecard needs illnesses to be logged; an illness that was never logged counts as a strain day with nothing after it.

references.citation: Ledoit O, Wolf M. A well-conditioned estimator for large-dimensional covariance matrices. J Multivar Anal 2004;88(2):365-411.

metrics.methodology: A randomised N-of-1 test, registered before the first day: the outcome (one primary, at most three secondary), the smallest change that would matter (the no-effect zone) and the schedule are fixed when the person registers, and the database refuses later changes and a schedule that starts in the past. Two designs. Periods in random order (a supplement or a fueling product): pairs of equal periods, with and without, the order inside each pair drawn on the phone (SecureRandom); every period starts with a washout whose days do not count. Each pair gives one difference (with minus without, weekday-adjusted, from its own two periods, so a slow drift cancels); the estimate is the mean of the pair differences with a Student t interval on them, and with six or more pairs the exact randomisation p over all the orders that could have been drawn. Days in random order (a same-day choice from the evidence board, such as no caffeine after 14:00): each week 3 or 4 days drawn for the rule, the outcome read the next morning; analysed as drawn, with an exact randomisation test that re-draws the schedule the way the phone did, and the interval from inverting it. The answer, once the last period or day has been read, is CLEAR BENEFIT or CLEAR HARM (the 95% interval lies beyond the zone, in the outcome's favourable or unfavourable direction), NO MEANINGFUL EFFECT (inside it) or UNCLEAR (across an edge); while it runs the numbers are interim and carry no verdict. The days a period leaves out (illness; alcohol in the period designs) are frozen the night after it ends. Adherence comes from the supplement log or, for a daily rule, from what the check-in recorded. Optional blinding: a partner fills a weekly organiser with the real thing or a placebo following the schedule, and the app keeps the schedule out of sight. Plans registered before October 2026 used a fixed without-then-with order and keep their original reading.
limitations: It answers for this person, under the conditions tested, and says nothing about other people.
Unblinded, knowing which period or day it is can still move a self-rated outcome (energy, mood); the randomised order protects against trends, seasons and bad weeks, not against expectation.
Days or periods where the schedule was not followed still count as drawn, which shrinks a real effect toward zero; low adherence is reported with the result.
Slow-acting changes need longer periods: an effect that lingers beyond the washout leaks into the next period and also shrinks the difference.
Small designs can only see large effects: four pairs of 14 days see about 16% on HRV; the sheet shows what a design can detect before it is registered, and UNCLEAR is not evidence of no effect.

references.citation: Guyatt GH, Keller JL, Jaeschke R, Rosenbloom D, Adachi JD, Newhouse MT. The n-of-1 randomized controlled trial: clinical usefulness. Our three-year experience. Ann Intern Med 1990;112(4):293-299.
Klasnja P, Hekler EB, Shiffman S, et al. Microrandomized trials: an experimental design for developing just-in-time adaptive interventions. Health Psychol 2015;34(Suppl):1220-1228.
Edgington ES, Onghena P. Randomization Tests. 4th ed. Chapman & Hall/CRC; 2007.

metrics.methodology: A lookup against a small, hand-curated registry of supplement and drug pairs, each with a mechanism, an effect, advice, a minimum gap in hours where timing matters, and a primary citation (PubMed ID or DOI, or a product label). A roster item takes part in a pair when its product's ingredient keys match, or when a whole word of its name or ingredient names matches the registry's aliases. Pairs are unordered. Each pair is placed on your roster's time slots (morning 08:00, afternoon 13:00, night 21:00, the clock taken the short way round) and reported as same slot, too close, spaced, applies whenever both are taken, or a missing partner; as-needed items have no slot and are reported as unknown timing. A helpful pairing is shown only when both items share a slot. Entries whose citations nobody has checked yet are labelled "(unreviewed)" next to the effect text.
limitations: Not medical advice and not a complete list: only the pairs in the registry are checked, and an absence of a flag does not mean a combination is safe.
Slots are nominal clock times; the real gap depends on when you actually take each item. Advised gaps marked as a precaution in the entry are not figures from the cited study.
Doses are not compared (the roster stores free-text doses), so an entry about high total intake, such as long-term zinc without copper, appears whenever the pair is present, whatever the dose.
A single product that contains both sides of a pair is not flagged against itself.
Where a prescription medicine is involved, the product label and your prescriber decide; the registry only prompts the question.

metrics.methodology: A general grade shown only on the User profile page. Eight factors are each placed as favorable, neutral or opportunity, or left unassessed: cardio fitness (VO2max percentile for your age and sex), biological age (PhenoAge versus calendar age), strength (the median level of your main barbell lifts, from your best estimated one-rep max in the last six months against bodyweight multiples used by lifters; needs at least three lifts and a body weight from the last 90 days), body composition (waist-to-height ratio), sleep (average duration over the last 30 days with the sleep regularity index), activity (median daily steps over the last 30 days against the Tudor-Locke and Bassett categories), blood lipids (triglycerides and HDL against the harmonised metabolic syndrome criteria) and blood glucose (HbA1c, or fasting glucose when there is no valid HbA1c, against the American Diabetes Association categories). A factor is assessed only when every input passes a trust gate: present, recent (labs within a year, VO2max within 90 days), enough days of data, confidence met, a known matching unit, no conflicting values for the same marker on the same date, and nothing assumed; sleep and steps restart at a confirmed series break. The grade is the share of assessed factors that are favorable, shown as a letter (A at 80% or more, B at 60%, C at 40%, otherwise D) only when at least five factors are assessed; below that it is labelled preliminary. The cut-offs for cardio fitness, biological age, the regularity index and the letter bands are product-defined. Handgrip readings you log are shown beside the strength factor but are not scored, because no cited norm table is installed.
limitations: Product-defined and provisional, not clinically validated: the cut-offs, the letter bands and the minimum of five assessed factors have not been tested against outcomes, and with only a few lab draws they cannot yet be checked on your own history.

The strength factor uses lifter standards (bodyweight multiples), not population percentiles, and they are not adjusted for sex or age; an estimated one-rep max from a set of several reps is an estimate.
A factor that cannot be assessed is left out, not scored as bad, so the grade describes only the factors you have data for and can move a lot when one more becomes assessable.
Blood pressure, family history, smoking, diet and many other determinants of healthspan are not inputs; a favorable grade does not mean low risk.
Long sleep is not penalised (only under 7 hours counts against duration), and a single panel or reading is treated as current for a year.
Lab values come from the panels you entered and are as accurate as that entry; the grade does not replace a clinician's reading of them.

references.citation: Mandsager K, Harb S, Cremer P, et al. Association of cardiorespiratory fitness with long-term mortality among adults undergoing exercise treadmill testing. JAMA Netw Open 2018;1(6):e183605.
Levine ME, Lu AT, Quach A, et al. An epigenetic biomarker of aging for lifespan and healthspan. Aging (Albany NY) 2018;10(4):573-591.

Ashwell M, Gunn P, Gibson S. Waist-to-height ratio is a better screening tool than waist circumference and BMI for adult cardiometabolic risk factors: systematic review and meta-analysis. Obes Rev 2012;13(3):275-286.

Watson NF, Badr MS, Belenky G, et al. Recommended amount of sleep for a healthy adult: a joint consensus statement of the American Academy of Sleep Medicine and Sleep Research Society. Sleep 2015;38(6):843-844.
Windred DP, Burns AC, Lane JM, et al. Sleep regularity is a stronger predictor of mortality risk than sleep duration: a prospective cohort study. Sleep 2024;47(1):zsad253.
Tudor-Locke C, Bassett DR Jr. How many steps/day are enough? Preliminary pedometer indices for public health. Sports Med 2004;34(1):1-8.

Alberti KGMM, Eckel RH, Grundy SM, et al. Harmonizing the metabolic syndrome: a joint interim statement of the IDF Task Force on Epidemiology and Prevention; NHLBI; AHA; WHF; IAS; and IASO. Circulation 2009;120:1640-1645.
American Diabetes Association Professional Practice Committee. 2. Diagnosis and classification of diabetes: Standards of Care in Diabetes-2025. Diabetes Care 2025;48(Suppl 1):S27-S49.

metrics.methodology: Each morning is compared with a forecast made before it: a slowly moving level plus a weekly pattern (exponential smoothing, ETS(A,N,A)) fitted to your own readings, HRV on a log scale. The band's width is the spread of recent one-step errors, widened after missing days and while errors are few (Student t). The 80% band should hold about 8 mornings in 10; how often it actually did is shown. A flag needs a morning beyond the 99% band, or several mornings on one side that trip an EWMA chart (lambda 0.3, limit 2.4). A confirmed device change starts a new regime.
limitations: One morning outside the 80% band is ordinary: about 1 in 5 mornings is, by design.
The weekly pattern and level absorb habits that repeat (a weekend routine), so a regular habit's effect sits inside 'expected'; the evidence board looks at those.
Needs about seven weeks of readings, and starts again (wide at first) after a confirmed device change.

references.citation: Hyndman RJ, Koehler AB, Ord JK, Snyder RD. Forecasting with Exponential Smoothing: The State Space Approach. Springer; 2008.
Lucas JM, Saccucci MS. Exponentially weighted moving average control schemes: properties and enhancements. Technometrics 1990;32(1):1-12.

metrics.methodology: Each occurrence (the first evening of a run) is lined up with the three days before and five after. Each day's distance from what the expected-band model forecast from before the window is compared with the same days around evenings on the same weekday without it. The grey chance band reassigns which days count as events within each weekday (400 times) and is simultaneous across the days shown, so with no effect the whole curve stays inside it 95% of the time. Drawn from 8 events.
limitations: Consecutive evenings count as one episode, so the curve shows the episode, not one evening.
Other things that happen on the same evenings (late nights, travel) are part of what the curve shows.
A day before the event outside the band means the outcome already differed: something else may drive both.

references.citation: MacKinlay AC. Event studies in economics and finance. J Econ Lit 1997;35(1):13-39.

metrics.methodology: Starting from mornings outside the 80% expected band on the unfavourable side, the evening before is compared with the evenings before reference days on the same weekday in the same calendar month (time-stratified case-crossover). Each low morning is its own control, so stable habits cancel out. Mantel-Haenszel odds ratio with the Robins-Breslow-Greenland 95% interval; shown from 15 low mornings with a known exposure.
limitations: Exploratory: several exposures are screened at once, so a row is a hint of what to test next, not an answer.
Assumes the exposure's effect is short-lived (a day).
Evenings with an unknown exposure are left out of both sides.

references.citation: Maclure M. The case-crossover design: a method for studying transient effects on the risk of acute events. Am J Epidemiol 1991;133(2):144-153.
Janes H, Sheppard L, Lumley T. Case-crossover analyses of air pollution exposure data: referent selection strategies and their implications for bias. Epidemiology 2005;16(6):717-726.

metrics.methodology: A distributed-lag regression: the outcome against the amount of the exposure on each of the seven days before (training minutes, steps, drinks), adjusted for weekday and a slow trend, with Newey-West standard errors. Each day's effect has its own 95% interval; how long it lasts is the first unbroken run of days whose interval excludes zero. For alcohol, a dose curve groups next mornings by drinks the evening before.
limitations: Needs 120 days with a full week of the exposure recorded behind them and at least 20 days with it.
Days with an unknown amount are left out, which for drinks means days without an answered check-in.
A smoothness constraint across days was tried and spread a one-day effect over the week, so each day is estimated freely and intervals are wider.

references.citation: Gasparrini A, Armstrong B, Kenward MG. Distributed lag non-linear models. Stat Med 2010;29(21):2224-2234.

metrics.methodology: An intervention read once, on a date fixed when it started (four weeks after the start unless the person set another, and never after it stopped), against a forecast from before it: the level and weekly pattern of the eight weeks before the start (HRV on a log scale) are carried forward over the days since, and the estimate is the average gap between what happened and that forecast. Its 95% interval counts neighbouring days as one long-run variance of the pre-period's day-to-day noise (lag-one autocorrelation, bias-corrected) for both the forecast's level and the gaps, with a Student t. The gap is judged against the outcome's no-effect zone: CLEAR, NEGLIGIBLE or UNCLEAR. A confirmed device change before the start shortens the pre-period to the days after it; one after the start leaves nothing to read. The read is published once and kept.
limitations: It is the OBSERVED rung: what happened against what was expected, not what the intervention did; anything else that changed at the same time counts too, and it never changes a protocol on its own.
The forecast assumes the eight weeks before would have stayed level; when they were already drifting the result says so.
Four weeks of an intervention only show large changes (about 16% on HRV is seen three times in four); a randomised self-experiment is the way to a tested answer.

references.citation: Bernal JL, Cummins S, Gasparrini A. Interrupted time series regression for the evaluation of public health interventions: a tutorial. Int J Epidemiol 2017;46(1):348-355.

metrics.methodology: Handgrip strength on a hand dynamometer, the best of three squeezes per hand, standing with the arm at the side and the elbow straight, alternating hands. Logged on its own or as the first step of the monthly body check-in.
limitations: Dynamometers differ from each other; readings from a different device are not comparable.
Posture and effort change the reading; the protocol is fixed so months are comparable, not so the number matches a clinic's.

references.citation: Roberts HC, Denison HJ, Martin HJ, et al. A review of the measurement of grip strength in clinical and epidemiological studies: towards a standardised approach. Age Ageing 2011;40(4):423-429.

metrics.methodology: Tape girths taken by the person at the monthly body check-in: neck, shoulders, chest, waist at the navel, waist midway between the lowest rib and the top of the hip bone (WHO site), hips, and on both sides relaxed upper arm (optionally flexed), forearm, mid-thigh and calf. A non-stretch tape, level, snug without compressing the skin, trunk sites at the end of a normal breath out. Two readings per site, a third when they differ by more than 0.5 cm; the value is the median. A change between check-ins, and a left-right difference, is called only beyond 2.77 typical errors of the site's value: the typical error of one reading from the within-sitting repeats, divided by the root of the readings behind the value, never below 0.5 cm.
limitations: Self-measurement is less reliable than a trained measurer; shoulders and chest in particular need a mirror or a helper to keep the tape level.
Within-sitting repeats miss the error of finding the landmark again on another day; the 0.5 cm floor stands in for it until enough months exist.
Food, fluid and the time of day move the waist by about a centimetre: the same conditions each month matter more than the tape.

references.citation: Stewart A, Marfell-Jones M, Olds T, de Ridder H. International Standards for Anthropometric Assessment. International Society for the Advancement of Kinanthropometry, Lower Hutt, 2011.
Hopkins WG. Measures of reliability in sports medicine and science. Sports Med 2000;30(1):1-15.
World Health Organization. Waist circumference and waist-hip ratio: report of a WHO expert consultation, Geneva, 8-11 December 2008. WHO, 2011.

metrics.methodology: Sum of three skinfolds the person can pinch on themselves, on the right side: abdominal (vertical, 2 cm right of the navel), suprailiac (diagonal, above the hip bone in line with the front of the armpit) and front thigh (vertical, seated with the knee bent). Three readings per site taken in rounds, a fourth when they span more than 2 mm; the value is the median. The caliper is recorded and a sum taken with a different caliper is not compared. The change is judged against the sites' typical errors added in quadrature (never below 1 mm per site), times 2.77. The sum is the primary skinfold number: it tracks subcutaneous fat without a population equation.
limitations: Self-pinched folds are less reliable than a trained measurer's; the same person, side, sites and caliper keep it comparable over time.
Cheap plastic calipers read differently from spring calipers such as a Harpenden; readings only compare within one caliper.
The triceps fold (part of the usual women's three-site equation) cannot be pinched on oneself and is left out.

references.citation: Stewart A, Marfell-Jones M, Olds T, de Ridder H. International Standards for Anthropometric Assessment. International Society for the Advancement of Kinanthropometry, Lower Hutt, 2011.
Hopkins WG. Measures of reliability in sports medicine and science. Sports Med 2000;30(1):1-15.

metrics.methodology: Waist (the WHO midpoint site, else at the navel) divided by height, from the monthly body check-in; waist-to-hip uses the same waist over the hips. Under 0.5 is the boundary the evidence supports for cardiometabolic risk.
limitations: A screening ratio, not a diagnosis.
Inherits the waist measurement's day-to-day error of about a centimetre.

references.citation: Ashwell M, Gunn P, Gibson S. Waist-to-height ratio is a better screening tool than waist circumference and BMI for adult cardiometabolic risk factors: systematic review and meta-analysis. Obes Rev 2012;13(3):275-286.

metrics.methodology: Two body-fat estimates from the monthly check-in, shown next to the scale's impedance reading and labelled as estimates: the US Navy circumference equation (men: waist at the navel minus neck, and height; women: waist plus hips minus neck, and height) and, for men who measured the chest fold, the Jackson-Pollock three-site skinfold equation (chest, abdominal, thigh and age) turned into body fat with Siri's equation.
limitations: Population equations: for one person each is typically a few percentage points off a reference method, and the methods disagree with each other.
Follow one method's trend; the gap between methods is not information about the body.
Needs sex (and age for the skinfold equation) in the profile.

references.citation: Hodgdon JA, Beckett MB. Prediction of percent body fat for U.S. Navy men and women from body circumferences and height. Naval Health Research Center, San Diego, Reports 84-11 and 84-29, 1984.
Jackson AS, Pollock ML. Generalized equations for predicting body density of men. Br J Nutr 1978;40(3):497-504.

metrics.methodology: Five zones placed three ways, switchable on a session's chart with a default in Training setup. % of maximum: zones start at 50, 60, 70, 80 and 90% of the maximum. Heart-rate reserve (Karvonen): resting + 50 to 90% of (maximum - resting). Lactate threshold (Friel's run zones): Z2 from 85%, Z3 from 90%, Z4 from 95% and Z5 from 100% of Zepp's lactate-threshold heart rate, for runs only. Auto uses the threshold for a run when Zepp has estimated one in the last 120 days, otherwise heart-rate reserve, otherwise % of maximum. The anchors are taken as of the session's date: the second-highest session maximum of the 24 months up to it, the 30-day median resting heart rate and the latest threshold estimate.
limitations: The maximum is the highest values the watch saw, not a tested maximum.
Zepp's lactate-threshold heart rate is an estimate from runs; it is not used for other sports.
Zone edges are conventions; the same bpm can be easy one day and hard on a hot or tired one.

references.citation: Karvonen MJ, Kentala E, Mustala O. The effects of training on heart rate; a longitudinal study. Ann Med Exp Biol Fenn 1957;35(3):307-315.
Friel J. The Triathlete's Training Bible. 4th ed. Boulder, CO: VeloPress; 2016.
Mann T, Lamberts RP, Lambert MI. Methods of prescribing relative exercise intensity: physiological and practical considerations. Sports Med 2013;43(7):613-625.

metrics.methodology: Each week's run, ride and hike minutes split as low (below zone 3), moderate (zone 3) and high (zones 4 and 5), from each workout's per-second heart rate placed in the zones of the default method with the anchors of its date. Only workouts with a Zepp heart-rate record are counted; the card says how many of the week's endurance sessions that is. Descriptive: endurance athletes typically spend about 80% of their training at low intensity, which the card mentions without setting a target.
limitations: Five zones folded into three bands approximate the three-zone model, which is defined by the two lactate or ventilatory thresholds.
Heart rate lags effort in short intervals, so time in the high band understates very short hard efforts.
Strength sessions are left out.

references.citation: Seiler S. What is best practice for training intensity and duration distribution in endurance athletes? Int J Sports Physiol Perform 2010;5(3):276-291.
